| angel-of-the-lord-speaks-as-god-identity-unstated / scope | Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readers have taken the angel as a messenger who speaks his sender’s words in the first person, as an appearance of God himself, or as a distinct divine person. The same alternation is found outside Genesis: at the bush the angel of the Lord appears and God calls (Exodus 3:2, 3:4), and Manoah, knowing he had seen an angel of the Lord, says they have seen God (Judges 13:21–22). | captain-of-the-host-of-the-lord-who-is-he / scope | Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the passage states: that the captain is an angel who commands the heavenly armies; that he is the Lord appearing in the form of a man, so that Joshua 6:2 continues the same meeting, a reading that points to the words about holy ground said to Moses at Exodus 3:5; that he is Christ before his birth, a reading held by some Christian interpreters. Limits on each: the Hebrew verb the KJV renders “did worship” here is the verb it renders “bowed himself” at Genesis 23:7, where it is done to men, so the verb alone does not show that the one bowed to is God, and a shared verb does not settle context; Revelation 22:8–9 has an angel refuse worship, which is quoted as a text used in this debate and not as an answer about Joshua; the passage does not say that the speaker of 6:2 is the captain. Brenton’s Greek of 5:14 as quoted has no word for “Nay” and no clause for “and did worship”; that difference is noted and not examined here. Check made: a search of the packaged KJV for “captain of the host of the Lord” and “captain of the Lord's host” finds Joshua 5:14 and 5:15 only; a search for “prince of the host” finds Daniel 8:11, which was not examined; Joshua 5:13–6:2 was read in the KJV. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses quoted state: that the woman’s practice brought Samuel up; that Samuel was sent apart from anything she did, which is offered as the reason for her cry; that what appeared was not Samuel, although the narrative uses his name. Limits: the narrative calls the one seen and the speaker “Samuel” at 28:12, 28:15, 28:16 and 28:20, and nothing in these verses says the appearance was false; only the woman is said to see, Saul asks her what she saw, and “Saul perceived that it was Samuel” follows her description; the woman’s words at 28:13 are her report, and the KJV’s “gods” there stands for a Hebrew word that the KJV elsewhere renders “God”, with a plural participle; 28:15 has Samuel say “to bring me up”, which states that he was brought up and does not say by whom; 1 Chronicles 10:13 in the KJV says Saul asked counsel of one that had a familiar spirit and does not say what answered, while Brenton’s Greek of that verse adds that “Samuel the prophet answered him”, a wording difference stated here and not proposed as a separate finding; Brenton’s Greek of 28:14 has “an upright man” where the KJV has “An old man”, and of 28:19 “with you shall fall” where the KJV has “be with me”, both also stated as wording only. Check made: 1 Samuel 28:3 and 28:6–25 were read in the KJV, verses 3 and 6–20 also in the Hebrew and the Greek; a search of the packaged KJV for “familiar spirit” finds Leviticus 19:31, 20:6, 20:27, Deuteronomy 18:11, 1 Samuel 28:3, 28:7, 28:8, 28:9, 2 Kings 21:6, 23:24, 1 Chronicles 10:13, 2 Chronicles 33:6, Isaiah 8:19, 19:3 and 29:4, and a whole-word search for “Endor” finds Joshua 17:11, 1 Samuel 28:7 and Psalms 83:10. Those are word searches and a reading of those verses, not a reading of the whole Bible. These checked verses do not explicitly settle by what means Samuel came up. No H or G is proposed. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. | what-became-of-shiloh-after-the-ark-of-god-was-taken / scope | Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses quoted state: that the Philistines destroyed Shiloh after the battle; that the place was left by the priests without being destroyed, and that what Jeremiah speaks of happened at a later time; that the forsaking in Psalm 78 is the loss of the ark and nothing more. Limits: Jeremiah 7:12 says something was done to “my place which was in Shiloh” because of wickedness and does not say what, when, or by whose hand; Psalms 78:60–61 joins the forsaking of the tabernacle of Shiloh to the delivering of “his strength into captivity” and does not describe the place afterwards; 1 Kings 14:2 and Jeremiah 41:5 speak of people at or from Shiloh in later times, so the verses quoted do not show the place empty for ever; at 1 Samuel 14:3 the words “the Lord's priest in Shiloh” may describe Eli and not Ahiah, and the verse does not say the priesthood was still at Shiloh in Saul’s time; 1 Samuel calls the house at Shiloh “the temple of the Lord” (1:9) and “the tabernacle of the congregation” (2:22), and whether the tabernacle later said to be at Gibeon (2 Chronicles 1:3) was moved from Shiloh, and when, is not told in the verses quoted; Brenton’s Greek of 2:22, quoted in full above, has no clause about the women or the tabernacle, a wording difference stated here and not proposed as a separate finding. Check made: a whole-word search of the packaged KJV for “Shiloh” finds, in 1 Samuel, 1:3, 1:9, 1:24, 2:14, 3:21, 4:3, 4:4, 4:12 and 14:3, and after 1 Samuel, 1 Kings 2:27, 14:2 and 14:4, Psalms 78:60, and Jeremiah 7:12, 7:14, 26:6, 26:9 and 41:5; each of those verses was read in the KJV, with 1 Samuel 4:3–4, 4:10–22, 7:1–2, 21:1–6 and 22:9–19; 1 Samuel 2:22 and 14:3 were also read in the Hebrew and the Greek. That is a word search and a reading of those verses, not a reading of the whole Bible, and a passage that tells of Shiloh without naming it would not be found by it. | michal-took-an-image-what-was-it-and-how-came-it-to-be-in-davids-house / scope | Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses quoted state: that it was a household figure of the kind Laban calls his gods; that it belonged to Michal and not to David; that it was a figure kept for some use other than worship; that it was large enough to pass for a man in a bed. Limits: a shared Hebrew word does not show that the object in David’s house was the same kind of thing as Laban’s or Micah’s, or that it was used as theirs were; the Hebrew word is plural in form in every verse quoted, and the KJV renders it “an image” here and “images” in Genesis, so its form does not settle whether one object or several is meant; the verses quoted do not say the object had a human shape or size — they say it was laid in the bed and covered, and that Michal said “He is sick”; Rachel sits upon hers (Genesis 31:34), which says something of the size of those and nothing of this one; the passage does not say David knew of the object, and it records no word of blame or of approval; no finding of a broken law is proposed, because the verses quoted do not describe any act of worship. The KJV’s “an image” for the Hebrew “the teraphim”, the KJV’s “idolatry” at 15:23, and Brenton’s Greek word at 19:13 are stated here as wording and are not proposed as separate findings. Check made: a whole-word search of the packaged KJV for “teraphim” finds Judges 17:5, 18:14, 18:17, 18:18, 18:20 and Hosea 3:4 only, so the English word does not lead to this passage; the Hebrew word was confirmed by script in the Westminster Leningrad text of 1 Samuel 19:13, 19:16 and 15:23, Genesis 31:19 and 31:34, Judges 17:5 and 2 Kings 23:24, and the Hebrew Bible was not searched for its other occurrences; 1 Samuel 19:8–18 was read in the KJV. That is a word search and a reading of those verses, not a reading of the whole Bible. These checked verses do not explicitly settle what the image was or whose it was. No H, G or V is proposed. | samuel-wrote-the-manner-of-the-kingdom-in-a-book-what-did-it-say / scope | Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses quoted state: that the book repeated the warning of 8:11–17; that it set out duties and limits of the king, like those of Deuteronomy 17:14–20; that it was an agreement between king and people. Limits: the same Hebrew noun in 8:9, 8:11 and 10:25 does not show that the same thing is meant, since 8:9 and 8:11 have “of the king” and 10:25 “of the kingdom”; Brenton’s Greek has “of the king” in all three verses, a wording difference at 10:25 that is stated here and not proposed as a separate finding; the Hebrew of 10:25 as pointed reads “in the book”, which Hebrew can use where English says “a book”, and the verse does not say it was a book already in being; Deuteronomy 17:18 speaks of the king writing a copy of “this law”, and the verses quoted do not say Samuel’s book was that law or that Saul made such a copy; the place where the book was laid up is given only as “before the Lord”. Check made: a search of the packaged KJV for “manner of the kingdom” finds 1 Samuel 10:25 only, and for “manner of the king” 1 Samuel 8:9 and 8:11 only; 1 Samuel 8:5–22, 10:17–27 and 12:1–25 and Deuteronomy 17:14–20 were read in the KJV, and 1 Samuel 8:9, 8:11 and 10:25 also in the Hebrew and the Greek. That is a word search and a reading of those verses, not a reading of the whole Bible, and a later mention of the book under another name would not be found by it. | because-he-slew-the-gibeonites-when-and-how-did-saul-slay-them / scope | Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses quoted state: that the killing took place at Nob, the city of the priests smitten in Saul’s reign (1 Samuel 22:19), on the view that Gibeonites served there as the “hewers of wood and drawers of water … for the altar” of Joshua 9:27; that it is connected with the flight of the people of Beeroth, one of the four Gibeonite cities of Joshua 9:17, told at 2 Samuel 4:3; that it was an act of Saul’s reign that no book narrates. Limits: 1 Samuel 22:19 names priests and a city and does not name Gibeonites; 2 Samuel 4:3 gives no cause for the flight and does not name Saul; “slew” at 21:1 and “sought to slay” at 21:2 can both be true of one campaign that killed some and aimed at all, so they are not set against each other here; that the event is not told does not show that it did not happen; the Greek of 21:5 has the added words “and pursued us”, a wording difference stated here and not proposed as a separate finding. Check made: 2 Samuel 21:1–14 was read in the KJV, verses 1–6 also in the Hebrew and the Greek; a whole-word search of the packaged KJV for “Gibeonite” or “Gibeonites” finds 2 Samuel 21:1, 21:2, 21:3, 21:4 and 21:9, 1 Chronicles 12:4 and Nehemiah 3:7; a search for “Gibeon” finds no verse of 1 Samuel; a search for “Beeroth” finds Deuteronomy 10:6, Joshua 9:17 and 18:25, 2 Samuel 4:2, 4:3, 4:5, 4:9 and 23:37, Ezra 2:25 and Nehemiah 7:29. | after-forty-years-absalom-forty-years-counted-from-what / scope | Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses quoted state: that the forty years run from an earlier event that the verse does not name, such as David’s anointing or the beginning of the kingdom; that the number was once a smaller one. Limits: both editions quoted have “forty” at 15:7, and no text with another number was examined in this session; the statement about Absalom’s birth rests on the condition that he was born while David reigned in Hebron, which 3:2–5 places there without giving a year; the chapters after 15 are not shown to stand in order of time, so the figure is not set here against the length of David’s reign as a contradiction; the vow of 15:8 is dated to the stay at Geshur, which 13:38 gives as three years, and that does not give the forty years a starting point. Brenton’s Greek of 15:7 has “to his father” where the KJV has “unto the king”, a wording difference stated here and not proposed as a separate finding. Check made: 2 Samuel 15:1–12 was read in the KJV, 15:7–8 also in the Hebrew and the Greek; a search of the packaged KJV for “forty years” in 2 Samuel finds 2:10, 5:4 and 15:7, and 2:10 gives the age of Ishbosheth. That is a word search and a reading of the verses quoted, not a reading of the whole book. These checked verses do not say from what the forty years are counted. No H or G is proposed. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses quoted state: that the old prophet wished to test whether the man of God would keep his charge; that he wanted the company or the honour of a man whose word had just been confirmed by a sign; that he acted for Bethel and its altar, to undo or discredit the message; that he sought a tie with the man of God for his own sake, in the light of his later request to lie in the same grave. Limits: the narrator’s words fix that the claim of an angel was a lie and do not describe the speaker’s purpose; the chapter records no reproof of the old prophet in the verses read, and that is not evidence of how the act was judged; the sentence at 13:21–22 is addressed to the man of God and names his own disobedience as its ground. The Greek of 13:31 has the added words “that my bones may be preserved with his bones”: that states a purpose for the burial request, not for the lie, and 2 Kings 23:18 reports that both sets of bones were left alone. | the-book-of-the-acts-of-solomon-what-was-it-and-where-is-it / scope | Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses quoted state: that the book was a record of Solomon’s reign kept at court, distinct from the later “chronicles of the kings”; that it is the same body of writing that 2 Chronicles 9:29 cites under the names of Nathan, Ahijah and Iddo; that it was a collection that held sayings as well as deeds, in view of “and his wisdom”; that it has not survived. Limits: the two books may point to different writings for the same reign without conflict, and no conflict is asserted here; that a title is found in one verse by a phrase search does not show that the writing is not meant elsewhere under another name; whether any existing writing is this book is not something these verses settle; the Hebrew word in the title can mean “words” or “acts”, and the KJV has “acts” for it in both halves of the verse. | a-writing-from-elijah-the-prophet-when-was-it-written-and-how-did-it-come / scope | Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the quoted verses state: that Elijah was still on earth, the order of telling in Kings not being the order of events; that Jehoram had begun to reign while his father lived, as 2 Kings 1:17 and 8:16 may suggest, and the killings fall in that time; that Elijah wrote beforehand and the writing was delivered later; that the writing came from Elijah after he had been taken up; that another man of the name is meant. What the verses do state is that a writing came, that it was from Elijah the prophet, and what it said. The words “poured water on the hands of Elijah” describe Elisha’s past service and do not by themselves say that Elijah was gone. | satan-came-also-among-the-sons-of-god-what-is-his-standing / scope | Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Possible readings: that Satan is here one of the sons of God whose part is to accuse or test; that he is an adversary of God who comes in uninvited or by permission; and that the word is a title for an office, not a name. Each is an interpretation; the verses quoted state none of them, in the KJV, the Hebrew or the Greek quoted, and this record asserts none. Zechariah shows Satan standing to resist a man before the angel of the Lord and being rebuked, and Revelation speaks of an accuser before God who is cast down; neither says what his standing was in the scene of Job 1 and 2. | genesis-9-humanity-from-noahs-family / reasoning | The scientific comparison concerns the recent, exclusive-family interpretation of the passage under ordinary inheritance. The genomic evidence supports a much older, structured ancestry; additional bottleneck analyses compare expected reductions in variation with multiple genetic systems. The paper is not a direct simulation of an eight-person flood bottleneck; the comparison draws on both its reconstructed history and the separately cited bottleneck analysis. The Adam-and-Eve references provide related context for an exclusive recent founding-couple reading. | This comparison tests a recent reading in which all people descend only from this family, through normal inheritance. DNA evidence supports a much older history with groups of ancestors. Other cited studies test how a sharp population fall would reduce differences across several kinds of DNA. The paper does not directly model an eight-person flood population. This comparison uses both its account of past populations and the separate study of a sharp population fall. The Adam-and-Eve sources give context for a recent reading in which all people descend only from one couple. | Keeps the exclusive recent-family assumption, ordinary inheritance, multiple genetic systems, and absence of a direct eight-person simulation. | Await owner acceptance. |
| genesis-9-humanity-from-noahs-family / scope | No minimum census population, precise bottleneck date or universally excluded ancestral couple is inferred. Effective population size is not a literal headcount. The cited study does not test miraculous creation or restoration of genetic diversity. | This does not infer a minimum headcount, an exact date for a sharp population fall, or exclude every ancestral couple. A genetic estimate of population size is not a literal headcount. A couple or family could be ancestors through family lines within a larger population; that is a different claim. Survival in one region, literary readings, and religious readings also make different claims. The cited study does not test miraculous creation or the miraculous return of genetic variety. | Preserves the census/effective-size distinction, genealogical ancestry alternative, regional/literary/theological alternatives, and miracle limit. | Await owner acceptance. |
